title: Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Judicial Evolution and Substantiation Standards in Federal Research Credits: A Post-Siemer Milling Co. Analysis
subject: Process of Experimentation
summary: Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2019-37) is a U.S. Tax Court decision applying IRC § 41 to a family-owned Illinois flour miller's research credit claims. The court sustained disallowance of all $238,670 claimed for TY 2011 and TY 2012 because Siemer never proved a hypothesis-driven process of experimentation, a key substantiation lesson for every R&D credit claimant.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Litigation and Procedural Posture

On April 15, 2019, the United States Tax Court handed down its memorandum opinion in Siemer Milling Company v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, T.C. Memo. 2019-37 (117 T.C.M. (CCH) 1196, Docket No. 21655-15), authored by Judge Ronald L. Buch. The decision, although a nonprecedential memorandum opinion, has become one of the most frequently cited decisions in United States federal research and development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41. Although the petitioner engaged in commercially valuable manufacturing process enhancements and product development initiatives across its commercial flour milling operations, the Tax Court sustained the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) disallowance of 100% of the claimed research tax credits for the fiscal tax years ended May 31, 2011, and May 31, 2012.

The ruling highlights a critical doctrinal divide in federal tax controversy between commercial or operational innovation in an industry sense and "qualified research" in a statutory and evidentiary sense. Following the issuance of Siemer Milling, practitioners reported that the IRS (including its Large Business and International (LB&I) division) was eager to rely on the decision in examinations to challenge credit claims that lack evidence of hypothesis-driven experimentation and supporting technical documentation. At the same time, Judge Buch's opinion established vital legal protections for taxpayers by rejecting overly narrow IRS litigating positions regarding multi-year technical uncertainties, combined product-and-process business component characterizations, and the asserted need for degreed engineers, and by finding reasonable cause that defeated the accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662.
Taxpayer Profile and Summary of the Claim

Siemer Milling Company ("Siemer") is a family-owned commercial wheat flour miller headquartered in Teutopolis, Illinois, that has operated continuously since the 1950s. During the fiscal tax years ended May 31, 2011 (TY 2011), and May 31, 2012 (TY 2012), Siemer owned and operated two commercial wheat milling facilities located in Teutopolis, Illinois, and Hopkinsville, Kentucky. To maintain competitiveness in the industrial food manufacturing sector, Siemer initiated several operational projects aimed at formulating new flour products, reducing microbial loads in raw and milled grain, stabilizing flour moisture levels, and evaluating novel milling machinery and wheat cultivars.

To quantify and claim federal R&D tax credits under IRC § 41, Siemer retained its long-standing public accounting firm, CliftonLarsonAllen LLP (CLA), which had prepared Siemer's corporate federal income tax returns for over two decades and was intimately familiar with its business operations. Relying on R&D tax credit studies that CLA prepared from employee interviews and Siemer-provided documents (as it had done since 2004), Siemer claimed federal research tax credits of $122,424 for TY 2011 and $116,246 for TY 2012. These credit claims aggregated qualified research expenses (QREs)—consisting primarily of in-house employee wages and supply costs—across seven distinct projects identified as business components (four projects for TY 2011 and five for TY 2012), only two of which—the Flour Heat-Treatment Project and the Pulsewave Project—spanned both tax years at issue. Specifically, the seven claimed business components were the Flour Heat-Treatment Project, the Ozone Project, the Hydration Project, the Pulsewave Project, the Wheat Hybrids Project, the Whole Wheat Flour Project, and the Littleford Day Project (a toasting project).

During the years in issue, Siemer's workforce spanned a wide spectrum of operational roles, including millers, maintenance personnel, laboratory technicians, laboratory supervisors, a research and development manager, and research and development staff; its vice president of production, Vernon Tegeler—who oversaw the preparation of the credit studies, supplied the time estimates used in them, and was the only trial witness who had participated in the projects—devoted a significant portion of his work hours to the claimed projects. Crucially, during TY 2011 and TY 2012, Siemer did not employ any individuals holding the formal title of engineer or geneticist, nor did it employ any personnel holding academic degrees in chemical engineering, mechanical engineering, or computer science.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following an examination of Siemer's TY 2011 and TY 2012 corporate income tax returns, the Commissioner issued a statutory notice of deficiency on July 15, 2015, disallowing 100% of the claimed research credits ($122,424 for TY 2011 and $116,246 for TY 2012) on the ground that Siemer had not proven that its expenses qualified, alongside unrelated adjustments to bonus depreciation, repair-cost capitalization, and depreciation schedules; the 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) were not determined in the notice but were asserted later in the Commissioner's first amendment to answer, so the Commissioner bore the burden of proof on them. The IRS's legal and factual challenge rested on five primary arguments.

First, the Commissioner asserted that none of the seven projects satisfied all four cumulative statutory requirements necessary to constitute "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1). Second, the IRS contended that the record was devoid of evidence that Siemer formulated or tested hypotheses, engaged in modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error, or evaluated alternatives, and that because Siemer employed no one with an engineering title or degree and called only one witness with direct knowledge of the research, it could not show reliance on hard sciences—urging the Court to draw an adverse inference from Siemer's failure to call other employees. Third, as a threshold legal theory, the Commissioner argued that a business component and its underlying technical uncertainty must be newly conceived within the specific tax year for which the credit is claimed. Because several of Siemer's projects and technical uncertainties carried over from TY 2011 into TY 2012 (or originated in prior tax periods), the IRS argued that confronting the same technical uncertainty across multiple tax years automatically disqualified the research. Fourth, the IRS argued that Siemer failed the business component test because Mr. Tegeler, when asked whether the business components related to processes or products, stated that they were all processes—whereas on brief Siemer described them as process improvements, product improvements, or both—and because the credit studies claimed more business components than Siemer presented at trial; at trial Mr. Tegeler described the projects as "processes that we worked with to develop products," a description the Commissioner treated as evidence of inconsistency in Siemer's identification of its business components. Fifth, the IRS challenged the evidentiary sufficiency of Siemer's case: it raised hearsay objections to 19 of the 113 stipulated documents (including the credit studies, which—apart from their wage summaries—were admitted only subject to those objections and not for the truth of the matters asserted), argued that Siemer's assertions regarding the substantially all requirement were conclusory, and argued that Siemer had not substantiated its fixed-base percentage, which CLA had computed from employee-interview estimates because the relevant base-year records could not be found.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The statutory framework governing Siemer Milling centers on IRC § 38 and § 41, operating in conjunction with IRC § 174 and the recordkeeping mandates of IRC § 6001. Under IRC § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer carrying on a trade or business is permitted to claim a credit equal to 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year over a statutory base amount derived from historical research spending and gross receipts. Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3), QREs encompass "in-house research expenses"—specifically employee wages paid or incurred for qualified services (engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or directly supervising or directly supporting such research) and amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research—as well as 65% of eligible "contract research expenses" paid to third parties.

For wages, supplies, or contract expenditures to constitute QREs, the underlying research activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1), which imposes a cumulative Four-Part Test that must be applied separately to each distinct "business component" pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(2)(A).

The first requirement is the Section 174 Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), which mandates that expenditures with respect to the activity must be eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process. Furthermore, as explained in Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582, 590-591 (1964), aff'd, 357 F.2d 209 (5th Cir. 1966) (as cited through Union Carbide in Siemer Milling), whether a taxpayer faces uncertainty is an objective test that depends on the information available to the taxpayer; in addition, under IRC § 174(e) expenditures qualify only to the extent they are reasonable under the circumstances, and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)(i) excludes the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control. While IRC § 174(a)(1) permitted immediate expensing during the 2011 and 2012 tax years at issue in Siemer Milling, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (Pub. L. No. 115-97, § 13206) subsequently mandated five-year domestic and fifteen-year foreign capitalization and amortization for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, until the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of July 4, 2025, enacted IRC § 174A to restore immediate domestic deductibility while retaining the substantive definition of § 174 research uncertainty.

The second requirement is the Technological Information Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), which dictates that the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is "technological in nature". Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. A taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor must the research succeed, provided the investigative process itself fundamentally relies on hard science principles.

The third requirement is the Business Component Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B), which requires that the taxpayer intend the application of the discovered technological information to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) defines a "business component" as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Additionally, IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) provides a special rule for production processes, stating that any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component and not as part of the product being produced. Where an overall business component fails the Four-Part Test, the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) instructs that the four tests be applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product or process until either a qualifying sub-component is isolated or the most basic element of the product or process fails to qualify.

The fourth requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), which mandates that substantially all of the activities of the research constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a qualified purpose. Under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B), a purpose is qualified if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, and is not related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Relying on Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court in Siemer Milling analyzed this fourth requirement across three distinct sub-elements: (1) the "process of experimentation" element, which under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) requires a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset, and which under Union Carbide "must involve a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense"; (2) the "substantially all" element, which under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) requires that 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for each business component, measured on a cost or other reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose; and (3) the "qualified purpose" element.

Finally, IRC § 41(d)(4) bars eight statutory categories of activity from qualifying for the credit, including research conducted after the beginning of commercial production under § 41(d)(4)(A), adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need under § 41(d)(4)(B), duplication of an existing business component under § 41(d)(4)(C), routine testing or inspection for quality control under § 41(d)(4)(D), and research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity under § 41(d)(4)(H).
The Tax Court's Final Holding

Judge Buch's opinion in Siemer Milling yielded a nuanced judicial outcome that rejected several of the Commissioner's restrictive legal theories while ruling entirely in favor of the IRS on the factual and evidentiary disallowance of the research credits.

On the threshold legal disputes, the Tax Court rejected the Commissioner's contention that a business component or its underlying technical uncertainty must be newly conceived and resolved within a single tax year. The Court held that neither IRC § 41 nor the Treasury Regulations prohibit a business component or a technical uncertainty from spanning multiple tax years, noting that "not all uncertainties are neatly resolved within the confines of a single taxable year". Similarly, the Court rejected the IRS's argument that Siemer's descriptions of its business components were inconsistent, holding that Mr. Tegeler's trial testimony describing the projects as "processes that we worked with to develop products," was not at odds with Siemer's characterization of the projects as process improvements, product improvements, or a combination of both, and did not bar Siemer from meeting its burden on the business component test for the projects presented at trial; the Court likewise held that the development or improvement of a business component can span more than one tax year. Only on the Wheat Hybrids Project did the Court find a failure of the business component test, holding that Siemer was merely testing existing hybrids developed by third-party breeders and growers rather than developing a new or improved product or process of its own.

On the substantive qualification of the seven projects, however, the Tax Court held that Siemer failed to satisfy its burden of proof on every single project claimed. None of the seven projects satisfied the Process of Experimentation Test; in addition, the Pulsewave Project (both years), the Littleford Day Project, and the Whole Wheat Flour Project failed the Technological Information Test, the TY 2011 Pulsewave Project also failed the Section 174 Test, and the Wheat Hybrids Project failed the Business Component Test. Having found no qualified research, the Court did not reach the Commissioner's challenge to Siemer's fixed-base percentage. Because Siemer failed to demonstrate that it engaged in a scientific process of experimentation on any business component, it automatically failed to prove that "substantially all" (at least 80%) of its claimed research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

Despite sustaining the 100% disallowance of the claimed research credits, the Tax Court held that Siemer was not liable for accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a), and it denied the Commissioner's motion to reopen the record to admit evidence of written supervisory approval under IRC § 6751(b), because that evidence would not have changed the outcome. Applying the reasonable cause and good-faith standard of IRC § 6664(c) and the three-prong test of Neonatology Associates, P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43 (2000), the Court concluded that Siemer reasonably and in good faith relied on the professional advice of CLA, its long-standing accounting firm, to whom it had provided full access to its corporate records and personnel.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal and technical dissection of Siemer Milling demonstrates that the taxpayer's defeat was not necessarily caused by a lack of genuine engineering or food-science innovation within its mills; indeed, experienced R&D tax controversy practitioners noted after the ruling that Siemer's projects appeared to be genuine engineering initiatives that should have qualified had they been properly structured and substantiated. Rather, the disallowance stemmed from interrelated legal, technical, and evidentiary failures, discussed below together with contractual lessons drawn from later cases.
Absence of a Methodical, Hypothesis-Driven Process of Experimentation

The decisive legal deficiency across all seven claimed business components was Siemer's failure to prove that its activities constituted a "process of experimentation" under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Throughout the opinion, Judge Buch repeatedly invoked the strict evidentiary formulation established in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50. Under the Union Carbide and Siemer Milling standard, a process of experimentation "must involve a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense".

Siemer's evidence fell short of this standard because it merely chronicled operational steps taken in the mill or laboratory without demonstrating how those steps formed a structured scientific investigation. In the Hydration Project, for example, where Siemer sought to maintain a consistent level of moisture in finished flour by reintroducing moisture to finished flour using water into which ozone had been introduced, the Tax Court observed that "all it did was recite the steps in its process. It does not explain how its process is scientific". Across all seven projects, Siemer failed to prove that it formulated a specific scientific hypothesis prior to testing, designed a methodical series of trials to evaluate one or more technical alternatives, analyzed empirical data against that hypothesis, or iteratively refined and retested its hypothesis. When a taxpayer presents a chronological summary of operational actions—such as installing equipment, running grain through a mill, replacing a mechanical part, and testing the resulting flour—without documenting the governing hypothesis and systematic evaluation of alternatives, the Tax Court holds that narrating the steps of a process does not establish testing of a hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense.
Failure to Establish Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Operational Adjustment

Under the Section 174 Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and the threshold element of the Process of Experimentation Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a taxpayer must establish that at the outset of its research activities, the available information did not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that component. As subsequently reinforced in Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37 (citing Siemer Milling), uncertainty under IRC § 174 and § 41 does not exist merely because a skilled operator does not know the exact outcome of a routine adjustment prior to making it; rather, the uncertainty must require investigative activities in the experimental or laboratory sense to resolve.

In Siemer Milling, the Court found that the taxpayer's TY 2011 Pulsewave activities—directed at running the leased machine faster than 3,600 RPM—were not research and experimentation but were more akin to mechanical maintenance. In commercial flour milling, operators routinely adjust roller gaps, replace worn bearings or sifter screens, and modify water tempering intervals to account for seasonal variations in wheat harvests. Because data that the manufacturer, Pulsewave LLC, had provided to Siemer in 2009 already included wheat milling tests at speeds of up to 4,500 RPM and other milling applications at up to 5,000 RPM, and because Siemer did not explain how its improvements to the machine would help it develop or improve a product, the Tax Court concluded that Siemer failed to prove that it faced uncertainty in the TY 2011 Pulsewave Project; the Court did not rest any other project's disallowance on the Section 174 Test, it expressly acknowledged that Siemer faced uncertainty in the Wheat Hybrids Project, and it rejected the Commissioner's argument that the same uncertainty cannot persist across several years.
Deficiencies Under the Technological Information Test and Workforce Credentials

To satisfy the Technological Information Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the taxpayer must prove that its process of experimentation fundamentally relied on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. While the Tax Court acknowledged that Siemer's projects aimed at reducing bacteria and microorganisms in flour (the projects whose stated objectives included reducing bacteria, such as the Flour Heat-Treatment, Ozone, and Hydration Projects) relied on principles of biology, the Court found the Commissioner's argument that Siemer had not identified the principles relied upon persuasive as a general matter, and specifically held that Siemer failed to establish the principles of hard science upon which its activities relied in the Pulsewave, Littleford Day, and Whole Wheat Flour Projects.

The Commissioner sought to tie these failures to the composition of Siemer's workforce, but the Court rejected that argument, holding that nothing requires a taxpayer to employ or contract with someone with a specialized degree, that degrees may be a factor but no specific set of degrees is required, and declining to draw an adverse inference because the Commissioner had equal access to Siemer's employees as witnesses. During TY 2011 and TY 2012, Siemer did not employ anyone holding the title of engineer or geneticist, nor did it employ any personnel with academic degrees in computer science, chemical engineering, or mechanical engineering. Instead, Siemer's workforce included millers, maintenance personnel, laboratory technicians, laboratory supervisors, and R&D staff. Although neither IRC § 41 nor the Treasury Regulations mandate that researchers hold specific academic degrees, the absence of formally credentialed engineers or scientists on the payroll can, as a practical matter, increase the evidentiary burden at trial, requiring the taxpayer's contemporaneous records to explicitly connect shop-floor mechanical and milling tasks to underlying principles of physics, chemistry, biology, or engineering.
Project-by-Project Analysis of Disqualification Across the Seven Business Components
The Tax Court's independent examination of each of the seven claimed projects demonstrates how these legal and evidentiary failures operated to disqualify the entire claim.

In the Flour Heat-Treatment Project, Siemer sought to develop thermal treatment processes to produce (1) cake flour without the use of chlorine, (2) low-microorganism and low-bacteria flour without the use of chemicals, and (3) all-natural replacements for modified starches, heating flour for differing times and with various methods and testing its composition, functional characteristics, and microbiological content. Although the record established that Siemer set out to develop three new products with its heat-treatment facility, the Court held that Siemer failed to prove a process of experimentation because it was not clear how Siemer set out to do that or whether that process was a true process of experimentation involving a methodical plan to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest it.

In the Ozone Project, Siemer introduced gaseous ozone into various stages of the wheat milling process to produce a low-microorganism flour suitable for products that might not be baked, testing wheat samples at each stage and comparing them with untreated grain, and then testing the treated flour for composition, bacteria level, and flavor. The Tax Court found that Siemer explained the steps in its process but did not expand on what theory it may have been testing or how it refined its process based on the data collected. Without more in the record to establish a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest it, the Ozone Project failed the process of experimentation test.

In the Hydration Project, Siemer attempted to find a method to maintain a consistent level of moisture in flour, experimenting with a machine that reintroduced moisture to finished flour after milling and introducing ozone into the water used to hydrate the flour to control bacteria and mold growth. The Tax Court held that the project failed the process of experimentation test because all Siemer did was recite the steps in its process without explaining how that process was scientific.

In the Pulsewave Project, Siemer leased a Pulsewave resonance-disintegration machine from its manufacturer, Pulsewave LLC (lease dated August 9, 2009; placed in service February 2010)—a new technology for the milling industry that only Siemer was using—seeking in TY 2011 to increase the speed at which the machine operated and to learn the effects of processing different grains, load sizes, and already-milled flour, and seeking in TY 2012 to adjust moisture in finished flour, keep the wheat kernel's oil packet intact, produce ultrafine wheat and bran flours, and understand how speed, rotation, and flow rate affected milling. As a result of the testing, Pulsewave LLC made physical modifications to the machine, and Siemer's own adjustments included replacing the bearings. For TY 2011, the Tax Court held that Siemer's activities were more akin to mechanical maintenance than research and experimentation, that adjustments such as replacing the bearings did not constitute experimentation, and that the project failed the Section 174, technological information, and process of experimentation tests; for TY 2012, the project failed the technological information test because Siemer's claimed reliance on resonance disintegration to separate a wheat kernel along its natural growth pattern was conclusory, and it again failed the process of experimentation test.

In the Wheat Hybrids Project, Siemer tested new varieties of wheat hybrids obtained from third-party agricultural breeders and growers, milling them and testing the composition and product yield of each sample to determine whether they could be used in current or new products, and sharing the results with the breeders and its customers. The Tax Court held that this project failed both the Business Component Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Because external breeders developed the wheat varieties, Siemer was not developing a new or improved product or process of its own; rather, it was simply determining what was available from wheat breeders and growers; although the Court acknowledged that Siemer faced uncertainty about whether the hybrids would suit current or new products, it held that this testing was more akin to evaluating products available on the market under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example (5), than a true process of experimentation.

In the Whole Wheat Flour Project, Siemer sought in TY 2012 to produce an ultrafine whole wheat flour, attempting to use pearling machines to strip the bran layer, later reintroducing the ground bran into the flour during milling, and then testing bacteria content and other characteristics of the flour. Similarly, in the Littleford Day Project (a toasting project), Siemer, unable to produce toasted wheat and bran flours with its existing heat-treatment facilities, sought a system that could be incorporated into its mills and supplied flour, grain, and bran samples to Littleford Day, a third party that heat-treated or toasted them at varying times and temperatures. For both projects, the Tax Court held that Siemer failed the technological information test because it offered only conclusory statements about relying on principles of biology, engineering, biochemistry, or food science without explaining how those principles were relied upon, and failed the process of experimentation test because narrating its steps or stating that it ran tests did not show a hypothesis formed, tested, and retested; the Littleford Day Project also failed because the record did not show that the work was not simply an evaluation of a vendor's product, while the Court made no finding that either project lacked uncertainty (indeed, it found that Siemer was unsure how to produce an ultrafine whole wheat flour).
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation, Wage Allocation Defects, and Contractual Pitfalls

Compounding its substantive failures under the Four-Part Test, Siemer's claim was weakened by evidentiary deficiencies in its documentation (the recordkeeping obligations of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) supply the general framework, although the opinion did not rest on them). Although CLA's credit studies contained wage information and contemporaneous documentation—narratives of particular experiments, sample test orders, recipes used in testing flour products, and lab results—the Tax Court found that many of the documents were not dated and that their authors and sources were unknown; the credit studies were admitted only subject to the Commissioner's hearsay objections (with only the wage summaries later admitted as summary exhibits), and the Court stated that even if Siemer could have relied on them for the truth of the matters asserted, they would not have been enough to establish a process of experimentation. In practical terms, the record did not capture the specific "who, what, where, when, why, and how" linking individual employee activities to technical uncertainties and experimental trials.

Furthermore, because Siemer did not show that it engaged in a process of experimentation at all—and offered only conclusory statements on the point—it could not substantiate the "substantially all" (80%) requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). As the Tax Court stated directly in Siemer Milling—and as the Seventh Circuit later reasoned in a separate case involving the taxpayer's own vessel-construction projects, Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), a decision consistent with Siemer Milling—because the taxpayer failed to demonstrate that it engaged in a process of experimentation (and, in Little Sandy Coal, also relied on estimates that mixed ordinary production and construction work with research), it could not prove that at least 80% of the activities for each business component constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

Finally, Siemer Milling and its subsequent progeny highlight critical contractual and supply expense traps regarding third-party equipment, raw materials, and customer-funded engineering. First, when a taxpayer leases or buys commercial machinery, Siemer Milling illustrates the risk: in the Pulsewave Project, the manufacturer's own pre-lease test data already established the speeds Siemer sought, the physical modifications were made by the manufacturer, and Siemer's adjustments (such as replacing bearings) were more akin to mechanical maintenance; similarly, the Littleford Day Project failed in part because Siemer could not show it was doing more than evaluating a vendor's product—so practitioners advise that any taxpayer-led modification of vendor equipment be contractually authorized and documented (the opinion itself did not address lease terms or intellectual property rights). Second, under the Union Carbide supply doctrine and Stephens v. Commissioner (Docket No. 9920-21, citing Siemer Milling), raw materials (such as bulk wheat) processed during trial runs on a commercial line and subsequently sold to customers in the ordinary course of business cannot be claimed as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) unless they represent extraordinary experimental costs or true pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Third, where development projects are undertaken for commercial customers or alongside external partners, failure to structure contracts so that payment is contingent on technical success and the taxpayer retains substantial rights triggers the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), as thoroughly analyzed in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21 (citing Siemer Milling).
3. Comparative Summary Tables
Table 1: Mapping Statutory Requirements Against Taxpayer Failures and Judicial Standards of Proof

Table 1 maps each statutory and regulatory requirement examined in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner against the specific legal and evidentiary deficiencies in Siemer's presentation and the governing standard of proof enforced by the U.S. Tax Court.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Siemer Milling
Tax Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Business Component Identification

In the Wheat Hybrids Project, Siemer tested existing wheat hybrids developed by external breeders and growers rather than developing its own new or improved product or process. (In the other six projects, Siemer survived the IRS's general product-vs-process challenge.)

A taxpayer must prove that each claimed project seeks to develop or improve a distinct product, process, formula, invention, technique, or software of the taxpayer. Merely evaluating or selecting third-party commercial supplies/hybrids fails the business component test. However, a business component may validly span multiple tax years and encompass linked process/product improvements.
Section 174 Technical Uncertainty
IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1); Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582

Only the TY 2011 Pulsewave Project failed this test: Siemer did not prove uncertainty about the machine's achievable speed because the manufacturer's 2009 data showed tests at up to 4,500 RPM (wheat) and 5,000 RPM (other materials), and its activities were more akin to mechanical maintenance. The Court did not rest the disallowance of Whole Wheat Flour, Littleford Day, and Pulsewave (TY 2012) on this test, and it found that Siemer did face uncertainty in the Wheat Hybrids Project.

The taxpayer must prove through objective evidence that available knowledge at the project's inception could not establish capability, method, or appropriate design. While the Court rejected the IRS's argument that an uncertainty cannot span multiple tax years ("not all uncertainties are neatly resolved within the confines of a single taxable year"), the uncertainty itself must be technical and investigative, not operational routine.
Technological in Nature (Hard Sciences)

Aside from biological principles the Court acknowledged for projects shown to seek bacteria reduction (e.g., Ozone and Flour Heat-Treatment, Hydration), Siemer failed to establish how it relied on any specific principles of engineering, physics, chemistry, or biology—the Court expressly so held for Pulsewave (both years), Littleford Day, and Whole Wheat Flour. Siemer employed no titled engineers or geneticists and no degreed chemical/mechanical engineers.

The taxpayer must specifically identify and substantiate the exact principles of physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science upon which the investigation fundamentally relies. The Court held that no specific set of degrees is required (degrees may be a factor) and declined the Commissioner's requested adverse inference; as a practical matter, where a workforce consists of production operators and maintenance staff rather than degreed engineers, records should explicitly bridge shop-floor actions to hard science principles.
Process of Experimentation (Scientific Method)
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5); Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50

Across all seven projects, Siemer merely recited chronological steps in its process (e.g., Hydration Project), made adjustments akin to mechanical maintenance, such as replacing bearings (Pulsewave Project), or explained the steps of its sample testing without stating what theory it was testing or how it refined its process (Ozone Project) without formulating or testing scientific hypotheses.

Relying on Union Carbide, the Court requires proof of "a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense". Narrating the steps of a process, or stating that tests were run, is legally insufficient.
"Substantially All" (80% Rule) & Qualified Purpose
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); IRC § 41(d)(3); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6); Little Sandy Coal Co., 62 F.4th 287

Because Siemer failed to prove that it engaged in a process of experimentation on any project, and supported its R&D claims with only conclusory assertions on this point, it necessarily failed the 80% threshold.

At least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities for each business component (measured on a cost or reasonable basis) must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Failure to prove a scientific process of experimentation automatically causes a failure of the "substantially all" test.
Contemporaneous Substantiation & Nexus
IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1

Siemer relied on CLA credit studies (built from employee interviews and documents) whose contemporaneous materials—experiment narratives, test orders, recipes, and lab results—were often undated and of unknown authorship and source; apart from the wage summaries, the studies were admitted only subject to hearsay objections, and the Court found they would not have established a process of experimentation even if accepted for their truth. Only one witness who had participated in the projects (Mr. Tegeler) testified.

Taxpayers bear the burden of maintaining records in a sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that claimed QREs directly tie to qualified research activities per business component. Post-hoc narrative summaries without underlying empirical test logs and dated documentation fail under Tax Court scrutiny.
Accuracy-Related Penalties & Reasonable Cause
IRC § 6662(a); IRC § 6664(c)(1); Neonatology Associates, P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43 (2000)

The Commissioner asserted 20% accuracy-related penalties (for substantial understatement and negligence) in a first amendment to answer rather than in the notice of deficiency, following the total disallowance of Siemer's $238,670 combined research credit claims for TY 2011 and TY 2012; he therefore bore the burden of proof and moved to reopen the record to add evidence of written supervisory approval under § 6751(b).

The Tax Court rejected all penalties, holding Siemer not liable, and denied the motion to reopen the record because the evidence would not change the outcome. Under Neonatology, a taxpayer establishes reasonable cause and good faith by proving: (1) the adviser (CLA) was a competent professional with sufficient expertise; (2) the taxpayer provided necessary and accurate information; and (3) the taxpayer actually relied in good faith on the adviser's judgment.

body.text: Table 2: Project-by-Project Disposition Matrix in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner
Table 2 summarizes the factual parameters, specific evidentiary deficiencies, and judicial disposition for each of the seven claimed business components in Siemer Milling.

headers: Primary Evidentiary & Legal Deficiencies Identified by the Tax Court

cells: 1. Flour Heat-Treatment Project
Develop processes to produce cake flour without chlorine, low-microorganism/low-bacteria flour without chemicals, and all-natural replacements for modified starches.
Acknowledged reliance on biological principles, but record did not show how Siemer set out to develop its three target products or whether that was a true process of experimentation.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Process of Experimentation & Substantially All Tests.
2. Ozone Project
Introduce gaseous ozone into milling stages to oxidize bacteria and yield low-microorganism flour.

Siemer explained the steps in its process (introducing ozone at several stages and testing samples against untreated grain) but not what theory it was testing or how it refined its process based on the data.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Process of Experimentation & Substantially All Tests.
3. Hydration Project
Maintain consistent moisture levels in finished flour via moisture reintroduction and ozone integration.
Per the Court, all the taxpayer did was recite the steps in its process, without explaining how the process was scientific.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Process of Experimentation & Substantially All Tests.
4. Pulsewave Project

TY 2011: increase the leased resonance-disintegration machine's operating speed and learn the effects of processing different grains, loads, and already-milled flour; TY 2012: adjust finished-flour moisture, keep the kernel's oil packet intact, produce ultrafine wheat and bran flours, and study the effects of speed, rotation, and flow rate.

TY 2011: no proven uncertainty about speed (manufacturer data showed tests up to 4,500/5,000 RPM) and activities more akin to mechanical maintenance (e.g., replacing bearings), so TY 2011 also failed the Section 174 Test; both years: reliance on scientific principles (resonance disintegration) asserted only conclusorily, and no methodical plan of hypothesis testing.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Technological Information & Process of Experimentation Tests.
5. Wheat Hybrids Project
Test new wheat varieties from third-party breeders and growers to assess composition and product yield for current or new products.

Hybrids were developed by external breeders, not Siemer; Siemer was simply determining what was available from breeders and growers, and its testing was akin to evaluating products on the market (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example (5)), although the Court acknowledged that Siemer faced uncertainty.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Business Component & Process of Experimentation Tests.
6. Whole Wheat Flour Project
Produce an ultrafine whole wheat flour by using pearling machines to strip the bran layer and reintroducing the ground bran during milling.

Did not explain what scientific principles its testing relied on or how; stated that it ran tests without showing a hypothesis formed, tested, and retested (the Court found Siemer was in fact unsure how to produce the product).
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Technological Information & Process of Experimentation Tests.
7. Littleford Day Project
Find a system, tested through third party Littleford Day, that could be incorporated into existing mills to toast wheat and bran flours (existing heat-treatment facilities could not).
Conclusory claims of reliance on biochemistry, food science, and engineering; narrated process steps without hypothesis testing; record did not rule out mere evaluation of a vendor's product.
Disallowed (100%) — Failed Technological Information & Process of Experimentation Tests.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how United States corporate taxpayers and technical tax advisors can operationalize the holdings of Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner—alongside subsequent federal decisions citing Siemer Milling, including Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37, Stephens v. Commissioner, Docket No. 9920-21, and System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21—the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic projects confronting the exact legal traps that defeated Siemer Milling and detail step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Commercial Grain and Functional Food Ingredients Processor (Remedying the Ozone, Heat-Treatment, Pulsewave, and Wheat Hybrids Pitfalls)
Baseline Scenario and Identified Siemer Milling Vulnerabilities

Heartland Specialty Grains Corp. ("Heartland"), a mid-sized commercial grain processor and specialty flour manufacturer based in Illinois, intends to claim federal R&D tax credits under IRC § 41 and domestic research deductions under IRC § 174A for its 2026 tax year. Heartland is undertaking "Project PureGrain," an initiative to develop a continuous-flow, non-thermal gaseous ozone and pulsed-acoustic milling process capable of producing low-microbial, enzyme-stabilized ultrafine whole grain flour for ready-to-eat food manufacturers. In its initial, unstructured posture, Heartland leases a commercial acoustic disintegration mill from an equipment vendor (mirroring Siemer's Pulsewave Project), injects gaseous ozone into its tempering bins while testing microbial counts before and after milling (mirroring Siemer's Ozone and Hydration Projects), evaluates five new low-lipase wheat cultivars bred by an external seed company to see which cultivar yields the longest shelf life (mirroring Siemer's Wheat Hybrids Project), and assigns plant millers, maintenance mechanics, and quality assurance (QA) technicians to run trials on Production Line 2 while selling passing flour batches to commercial customers and claiming bulk wheat grain as supply QREs.

If examined by the IRS in this baseline posture, Heartland faces a 100% credit disallowance under Siemer Milling. Its seed testing fails the Business Component Test as mere vendor input evaluation; its acoustic mill modifications resemble the adjustments, such as bearing replacements, that Siemer Milling treated as akin to mechanical maintenance; its ozone microbial sampling looks like comparative quality control rather than hypothesis-driven experimentation; its shop-floor workforce lacks documented hard-science oversight; and its commingled commercial production runs violate both the "substantially all" (80%) requirement and the Union Carbide commercial inventory supply exclusion.
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Structuring

To cure the Wheat Hybrids business component defect identified in Siemer Milling, Heartland's tax and engineering leadership must formally bifurcate raw material screening from process development prior to project execution. All hours and material costs incurred by QA technicians evaluating third-party breeder cultivars to select a preferred commercial grain vendor are quarantined into a non-qualifying cost center designated as excluded vendor inspection under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). Heartland then defines its sole qualifying business component strictly under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) as a new plant manufacturing process—specifically, the Continuous-Flow Ozonated Acoustic Milling Process (Business Component ID: BC-2026-01)—targeted at achieving a specific functional and quality improvement: a ≥ 3.5 log CFU/g reduction in coliform and aerobic spore-forming bacteria while maintaining starch damage below 6.5 AACC units and lipid peroxidation (free fatty acid level) below 0.08%.

Simultaneously, to preempt the type of argument the Commissioner raised in Siemer Milling regarding the absence of titled or degreed engineers—an argument the Court actually rejected, holding that no specific degree is required although degrees may be a factor, Heartland charters an R&D Technical Steering Committee chaired by its Director of Food Science (holding an M.S. in Cereal Chemistry) alongside a retained Process Engineering Consultant (holding a B.S. in Chemical Engineering). Every experimental protocol executed on the mill floor by millers and maintenance technicians is authored and signed by the Cereal Chemist and Chemical Engineer, explicitly grounding the investigation in established principles of biochemistry (ozone oxidative cleavage of unsaturated lipids versus bacterial cell wall lysis), fluid mechanics (counter-current gas-solid mass transfer in vertical tempering columns), and mechanical engineering (acoustic frequency resonance and shear stress particle fracture).
Step 2: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Protocols

Before incurring QREs, Heartland executes a dated Technical Uncertainty and Design Charter within its electronic document management system. Rather than stating a vague commercial objective, the charter memorializes exact method and design uncertainties under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). First, regarding method uncertainty, while published literature indicates that static gaseous ozone exposure at 3.0 ppm over several hours reduces microbial loads in stored grain, available scientific knowledge does not establish whether a continuous inline tempering residence time of under 45 minutes can achieve a ≥ 3.5 log CFU/g reduction without triggering rapid oxidative rancidity of wheat germ lipids during high-energy milling. Second, regarding design uncertainty, available knowledge does not establish the appropriate internal rotor geometry, acoustic wave frequency (280 Hz to 420 Hz), and air-classification manifold design needed to fracture bran pericarp layers to a median particle size (D50) below 120 μm without exceeding a chamber temperature of 42°C, above which gluten proteins denature and ozone thermally decomposes.

To overcome Judge Buch's criticism in Siemer Milling that "all it did was recite the steps in its process" without explaining how the process was scientific, Heartland mandates that every trial run be recorded in a dated Scientific Experimentation Protocol and Data Log structured directly around the Union Carbide scientific method mandate. Prior to each trial, the Cereal Chemist records a formal hypothesis statement, such as testing whether introducing ozonated air at 4.5 ppm counter-current into a 13.5% moisture-tempered grain column for 30 minutes, paired with a 340 Hz acoustic rotor frequency and a custom 15° tapered stator ring, will achieve ≥ 3.5 log CFU/g microbial reduction while keeping flour exit temperature below 40°C and peroxide value below 2.0 meq/kg. During the run, technicians log all independent variables manipulated (ozone concentration, gas superficial velocity, tempering moisture, rotor frequency, and stator ring geometry) alongside empirical laboratory measurements (microbial enumeration in log CFU/g, laser diffraction particle size, megazyme starch damage assays, and peroxide values) compared against an untreated control batch. Immediately following the run, the log documents hypothesis evaluation and failure analysis—for instance, recording that Iteration 4 achieved a 3.8 log CFU/g microbial reduction but failed thermal criteria because chamber back-pressure spiked temperatures to 49.2°C and peroxide values to 4.1 meq/kg—followed by a refined hypothesis for Iteration 5 to machine auxiliary cooling air bypass louvers into the stator discharge manifold to increase volumetric airflow by 22% and retest at 320 Hz.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring for Leased Equipment and Experimental Supplies

In Siemer Milling, Siemer's adjustments to the leased Pulsewave machine, such as replacing the bearings, did not constitute experimentation, and the TY 2011 work was found more akin to mechanical maintenance—particularly because the manufacturer's own data already showed the speeds Siemer sought. To cure this defect, Heartland restructures its equipment lease with the acoustic mill OEM into a Technical Modification and Pilot Process Development Lease. The agreement explicitly states that the OEM's standard commercial machine is not rated or engineered for ozonated whole-grain sub-120 μm milling, grants Heartland the contractual authority to design, fabricate, and install custom experimental internal rotors, cooling manifolds, and ozone-resistant PTFE/Viton sealing assemblies at Heartland's sole technical and financial risk, and vests exclusive intellectual property ownership ("substantial rights" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) in Heartland for all process parameters, custom tooling modifications, and manifold designs developed during the lease term. Routine preventative maintenance—such as replacing worn factory bearings—is contractually and accounting-wise segregated from custom prototype fabrication.

Furthermore, to comply with the supply QRE doctrine of Union Carbide and Stephens v. Commissioner (citing Siemer Milling), under which raw materials used in normal operations and sold in the ordinary course of business are disqualified, Heartland constructs an isolated pilot-scale bypass loop off Production Line 2. All wheat grain processed during experimental Iterations 1 through 12 is strictly quarantined as non-commercial experimental test material, subjected to destructive microbiological and chemical testing, and disposed of as non-saleable bio-waste, tracked under a dedicated general ledger R&D supply account (GL 5410-RD-Supplies) completely separate from Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) commercial inventory.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Substantiating the "Substantially All" (80%) Rule

To avoid the failures of proof on the substantially all requirement seen in Siemer Milling and Little Sandy Coal, Heartland configures its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and payroll timekeeping system with granular activity codes linked directly to the dated experimental logs. Employees log time contemporaneously across three qualified codes—BC2026-01-EXP for direct performance of hypothesis formulation, engineering calculations, experimental mill modification, and executing logged trial iterations; BC2026-01-SUPV for first-line direct supervision by the Cereal Chemist during experimental runs; and BC2026-01-SUPP for direct support tasks such as machining experimental stator rings and sanitizing the pilot loop between iterations—while logging routine bearing swaps and commercial milling to excluded codes (NON-RD-MAINT and NON-RD-PROD). At year-end, Heartland substantiates the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) "substantially all" requirement for BC-2026-01 by dividing the 1,840 hours logged to BC2026-01-EXP by the 1,920 total research hours associated with the business component (which includes 80 hours of non-experimental baseline setup), establishing that 95.83% of the component's activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation while excluding all NON-RD-MAINT and NON-RD-PROD wages from QREs.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Finishing and Airflow Engineering Contractor (Remedying Mechanical Adjustment, Pilot Model, and Funded Research Pitfalls)
Baseline Scenario and Identified Siemer Milling and Progeny Vulnerabilities

Apex Thermal & Airflow Systems, Inc. ("Apex"), an industrial engineering and custom manufacturing corporation based in Indiana, engineers and builds custom industrial curing systems and high-velocity spray washers with integrated blow-off and cool-off stages for automotive and aerospace manufacturers. For tax year 2026, Apex plans to claim IRC § 41 research credits on "Project Vortex," the design and manufacture of a custom multi-stage ultraviolet (UV) and high-velocity air-knife curing system for an automotive OEM client. In its baseline state, Apex faces four severe legal vulnerabilities rooted in Siemer Milling and subsequent Tax Court and appellate rulings directly citing Siemer Milling (Stephens v. Commissioner, Docket No. 9920-21; System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21; and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287).

First, Apex relies on the "novelty heuristic" rejected in Little Sandy Coal and Siemer Milling (in Siemer Milling, the Pulsewave machine was a new technology for the milling industry, yet that novelty did not establish qualified research), claiming 100% of the wages of its shop welders, CAD drafters, and field installers on the theory that because the custom curing line has never been built before, the entire machine is a pilot model and a process of experimentation. Second, Apex defines the entire curing line as a single business component, even though only the supersonic air-knife nozzle manifold and the regenerative thermal exhaust recovery exchanger involve fluid-dynamic uncertainty, while the structural steel frame, conveyor drive, and electrical cabinet are standard commercial designs. Third, Apex's standard commercial proposal requires non-refundable progress payments based on time and materials incurred, omits quantitative acceptance testing contingencies, and assigns all project drawings to the customer, triggering the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Fourth, during shop commissioning and after shipping the system to the customer's plant, Apex mechanics replace fan bearings, adjust damper blades, and balance airflow, lumping those hours into its R&D claim in violation of the Siemer Milling Pulsewave bearing replacement holding and the IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) post-commercial production exclusion.
Step 1: Project Governance and Shrinking-Back Business Component Definition

Rather than claiming the entire custom curing line as a single monolithic business component—which would inevitably fail the 80% "substantially all" test under Siemer Milling and Little Sandy Coal due to the substantial shop labor required to weld standard structural steel frames and wire standard control panels (a risk most directly illustrated by Little Sandy Coal; in Siemer Milling, the taxpayer recited the shrinking-back rule but never argued its application, and the Court declined to apply it on Siemer's behalf)—Apex's VP of Engineering and Tax Director proactively apply the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) at project inception. Apex formally isolates and designates two specific sub-assemblies as its qualifying business components for Form 6765 Section G reporting: the Supersonic Coanda-Effect Air-Knife Nozzle Manifold (BC-2026-A) and the Regenerative Counter-Flow Thermal Exhaust Recovery Exchanger (BC-2026-B). All engineering, drafting, procurement, and shop assembly associated with the standard structural housing, conveyor drive, and commercial UV lamps are segregated and excluded at the outset as routine commercial production and customer adaptation under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)–(B).
Step 2: Contractual Architecture to Overcome the Funded Research Exclusion

To ensure that Apex's development of BC-2026-A and BC-2026-B is not disqualified as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), Apex's legal counsel restructures the commercial purchase agreement prior to execution, incorporating the contractual mechanics addressed in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21 (citing Siemer Milling). First, to establish that payment is contingent on the success of the research, the sales contract is drafted as a fixed-price, performance-contingent agreement governed by an explicit Indiana Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) choice-of-law provision (incorporating buyer rejection and refund remedies under Ind. Code §§ 26-1-2-711 and 26-1-2-719). The contract stipulates that all milestone payments are refundable advances contingent upon the custom sub-assemblies passing a quantitative Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) and Site Acceptance Test (SAT)—specifically, achieving 99.4% moisture blow-off at a conveyor speed of 45 ft/min with acoustic noise below 65 dBA and thermal energy recovery of at least 78%. If Apex fails to resolve the aerodynamic and thermodynamic uncertainties required to meet these thresholds, the customer is legally entitled to reject the equipment and demand a full refund of all payments made, placing the entire economic risk of failure on Apex. Second, to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the contract's Intellectual Property clause specifies that while the customer receives title to the physical unit delivered and a non-exclusive operating license, Apex retains exclusive ownership and "substantial rights" to all underlying engineering calculations, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models, nozzle geometries, and heat-exchanger designs, with full legal freedom to deploy those innovations for future clients without paying royalties.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Computational and Physical Experimentation

To satisfy the Union Carbide and Siemer Milling mandate of a "methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis", Apex institutes a two-stage engineering documentation protocol linking its Git/Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) repositories to Jira engineering tickets.

In Stage 1, prior to physical fabrication, Apex's mechanical engineers document iterative CFD simulations in the PLM repository. Each committed simulation iteration records the threshold aerodynamic design uncertainty, the specific fluid-mechanics hypothesis being tested (such as Iterations 1 through 9 systematically varying Coanda lip radius from 8 mm to 14 mm and nozzle slot width from 1.2 mm to 0.65 mm to prevent boundary-layer detachment and acoustic resonance), the simulated shear-stress and decibel outputs, the analytical reason the iteration failed target metrics, and the mathematical refinement applied to the subsequent iteration.

In Stage 2, rather than constructing the entire commercial oven and claiming shop-floor mechanical adjustments, Apex fabricates three experimental prototype nozzle manifolds (BC-2026-A Prototypes v1, v2, and v3) and tests them on an instrumented laboratory wind-tunnel bench. Dated test logs capture hot-wire anemometer velocity profiles, infrared thermal imaging gradients, and acoustic decibel readings across systematic pressure trials. Any routine mechanical adjustments during final commercial assembly—such as replacing fan bearings, aligning belts, or performing post-shipment field installation support—are explicitly flagged and excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and Siemer Milling.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Pilot Model Supply Segregation, and Audit-Ready Substantiation

Apex integrates its Workday timecards, Jira tickets, and PLM commit logs at the sub-component level (BC-2026-A and BC-2026-B). Within five working days of the close of each monthly sprint—and strictly within the tax year or within 90 days thereafter—engineers verify their exact time allocations and attach dated design quotes and test logs to each of the four statutory tests. For instance, where a Senior Thermal Engineer's contemporaneously logged records show 75% of his annual hours devoted to BC-2026-B CFD modeling and thermal lab testing, 20% devoted to post-shipment field installation support after customer delivery, and 5% devoted to administrative duties, Apex's tax compliance system automatically excludes the 20% post-commercialization field support and 5% administrative time, claiming exactly 75% of his Box 1 W-2 wages.

Simultaneously, specialty alloys and sensors purchased to fabricate the three experimental laboratory test-rig manifolds (Prototypes v1–v3) are charged to a segregated R&D Pilot Model Supply work order. Even if Prototype v3 successfully resolves the aerodynamic design uncertainty and is ultimately mounted into the commercial machine delivered to the client, Apex's contemporaneous engineering orders document—in direct compliance with Stephens v. Commissioner (citing Siemer Milling) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—that the sub-assembly was constructed specifically as a pilot model to evaluate design alternatives and eliminate technical uncertainty prior to commercial production, thereby preserving supply QRE eligibility while strictly excluding the steel and component costs of the commercial oven structure.

Table 3 contrasts the disqualifying baseline practices identified in Siemer Milling against the remedial compliance frameworks implemented in Case Studies 1 and 2.

headers: Remedial Protocol in Case Study 1 (Food & Grain Processing)
Remedial Protocol in Case Study 2 (Custom Industrial Engineering)

cells: Business Component Framing (IRC § 41(d)(2))
Claiming third-party wheat hybrid evaluations as R&D; reciting the shrinking-back rule without arguing its application to narrower sub-components.
Quarantining third-party cultivar screening as excluded QC; defining the inline ozonated acoustic milling process as a distinct § 41(d)(2)(C) plant process component.
Applying the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back rule upfront to isolate two specific uncertain sub-assemblies (BC-2026-A and BC-2026-B) from standard machine framing.
Hard Science & Technical Governance (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i))
Failing to explain how specific scientific principles were relied upon (the Court rejected any requirement of degreed engineers, though degrees may be a factor).
Establishing an R&D Technical Steering Committee led by a degreed Cereal Chemist and Chemical Engineer who author all experimental protocols.
Documenting aerodynamic, thermodynamic, and fluid-mechanical equations inside PLM/Git repositories managed by degreed Mechanical Engineers.
Process of Experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C))
Reciting chronological steps (e.g., adding moisture or ozone and testing samples) or making adjustments akin to mechanical maintenance, such as replacing machine bearings.
Implementing mandatory 5-part Union Carbide experimental logs recording formal hypotheses, manipulated variables, lab assays, failure analysis, and retests.
Coupling iterative CFD simulation commit logs (Iterations 1–9) with instrumented wind-tunnel testing of physical sub-assembly prototypes (v1–v3).
Contractual & Supply Structuring (IRC § 41(b)(2) & § 41(d)(4)(H))

Adjusting leased vendor equipment (Pulsewave) whose capabilities the manufacturer's data had already established, and outsourcing testing to a vendor (Littleford Day) without showing it was more than a vendor-product evaluation (the opinion did not address lease rights or supply QREs).
Executing a Technical Modification Lease retaining IP rights; running experimental grain in a dedicated non-commercial pilot loop excluded from COGS.
Incorporating state UCC refund remedies and FAT/SAT performance contingencies to bear economic risk (System Technologies); isolating pilot sub-assembly supplies (Stephens).
Time Tracking & "Substantially All" Proof (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6))

Conclusory substantially-all assertions unsupported by proof of a process of experimentation, with credit-study documents often undated and of unknown authorship (interview-based time estimates were used, e.g., for base-year calculations).
Bi-weekly ERP activity codes segregating direct experimentation (EXP), supervision (SUPV), and support (SUPP) from bearing maintenance (NON-RD-MAINT).
Automated linkage of Workday timecards, Jira tickets, and PLM commits with contemporaneous engineer sign-off, strictly excluding post-shipment field support.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Controversy and Compliance Practice

The United States Tax Court's decision in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, although a nonprecedential memorandum opinion, is widely cited as illustrating the demanding evidentiary threshold required to sustain federal research tax credits under IRC § 41. While the ruling confirms that taxpayers may legitimately pursue multi-year research projects addressing persistent technical uncertainties and may claim integrated process and product improvements—and while good-faith reliance on a competent accounting firm can shield a taxpayer from IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalties under the Neonatology doctrine—relying on penalty relief is no substitute for substantive qualification.

To withstand IRS examination and Tax Court scrutiny in the post-Siemer Milling and Form 6765 Section G business-component reporting environment, corporate taxpayers and their tax advisors must eliminate retrospective narrative reconstructions. Every claimed business component must be anchored by dated, contemporaneous documentation created during the tax year that explicitly articulates the threshold capability, method, or design uncertainty, identifies the governing principles of hard science, isolates non-qualifying vendor input evaluations and routine mechanical maintenance, and memorializes a structured, hypothesis-driven process of scientific experimentation.

metaDescription: Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37: all $238,670 in credits for 2011 and 2012 were disallowed for lack of a hypothesis-driven process.
